clues: A palpable transverse ridge on the anterior chest wall at the junction of the manubrium and body of the sternum.
It lies directly opposite the second costal cartilage and marks the posterior T4-T5 intervertebral disc level.
Clinicians use it as the reference landmark for counting ribs and intercostal spaces.
The lowest and outermost point of definite cardiac pulsation palpable on the anterior chest wall.
It is generated by the inferolateral tip of the left ventricle striking the thoracic wall during systole.
In a healthy adult, it is located in the left fifth intercostal space just medial to the midclavicular line.
A horizontal reference line situated halfway between the jugular notch and the pubic symphysis.
It passes posteriorly through the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra.
It intersects the pylorus, the hila of both kidneys, and the tip of the right ninth costal cartilage.
A surface landmark in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen.
It lies one-third of the way along a line drawn from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.
Maximal tenderness here is a classic physical finding in acute appendicitis.
A horizontal line joining the highest points of the left and right iliac crests across the lower back.
It crosses the spinous process of the fourth lumbar vertebra.
Clinicians palpate this line to identify a safe intervertebral level for lumbar puncture.
A palpable horizontal bar of cartilage in the anterior midline of the neck below the laryngeal prominence.
It sits at the C6 vertebral level and marks the beginning of the trachea and esophagus.
The common carotid artery can be compressed posteriorly against the transverse process at this level.
A groin surface landmark located halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.
It lies slightly medial to the midpoint of the inguinal ligament.
The femoral artery pulse is palpated directly at this point.
The direct continuation of the anterior tibial artery onto the top of the foot.
Its pulse is palpated immediately lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.
Absence of this peripheral pulse is an important clinical sign of lower-limb peripheral arterial disease.
